extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers studying algebraic geometry (and advanced undergraduates familiar with schemes and sheaves)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and exercises about sheaves on a distinguished affine base, the characterization and finiteness properties of quasicoherent and coherent sheaves, basic category-theoretic structure (QCoh an abelian category), Jordan–Hölder for modules, and the theory of associated points. Intended as textbook material for learning and checking facts/exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: sheaves on Zariski topology vs distinguished affine base
rubrics_metrics.description: For experts: (a) and (b) are describing an equivalence of categories between sheaves on the Zariski topology of X and sheaves on the distinguished affine base of X. (An OX-module 'on the distinguished affine base' yields an OX-module.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the sheaf on X from a sheaf Fb on the distinguished affine base via the 'sheaf of compatible germs' and show this construction gives restriction maps, identity, and gluability. Show that for base open U one has F(U)=Fb(U) and that the map is an isomorphism on stalks; an isomorphism on stalks gives a global isomorphism (Exercise 2.4.D). The key categorical hypothesis used is that the base of distinguished affines forms a filtered category of opens (or more generally the open sets form a filtered set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf of compatible germs construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Define for any open U the set F(U) := {(s_p)_p∈U : there exist base opens Up with p∈Up⊂U, sp∈Fb(Up), and compatibility sq = fq on overlaps} (i.e., compatible germs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction yields restriction maps and satisfies identity and gluability axioms of a sheaf. Use this to pass from data on the distinguished affine base to a genuine sheaf on X; check the empty set if desired. When U is in the base, the constructed F(U) recovers Fb(U).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of quasicoherent sheaves (6.2.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: An OX-module F is quasicoherent if and only if for each inclusion Spec Af ⊂ Spec A (a distinguished open inside an affine open), the natural map Γ(Spec A, F) ⊗_A Af → Γ(Spec Af, F) (equivalently the factorization coming from localization) is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: a quasicoherent sheaf is the data of one module for each affine open Spec A such that restriction to a distinguished open Spec Af is given by localization of the module. Use the universal property of localization (Exercise 1.3.D) to see the natural factorization and check α is an isomorphism for all distinguished opens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicoherent sheaf data viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf is (equivalent to) the data of one module for each affine open subset (a module over the corresponding ring), such that the module over a distinguished open Spec Af is given by localizing the module over Spec A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint allows many constructions to be handled 'affine-locally' and explains why many operations (taking kernels, cokernels, tensor products, injectivity/surjectivity tests) can be computed on affine opens. It also clarifies when sheafification is unnecessary for constructions involving quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product of quasicoherent sheaves (6.2.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F and G are quasicoherent sheaves on X and on an affine open Spec A we have Γ(Spec A, F)=M and Γ(Spec A, G)=N, then Γ(Spec A, F⊗OX G) ≅ M⊗_A N and on a distinguished open Spec Af the sections are Mf ⊗_{Af} Nf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic facts about localization and the universal property of tensor products to show the restriction maps correspond to localization maps M ⊗_A N → (M⊗_A N)_f ∼= Mf ⊗_{Af} Nf. This shows tensor products of QC sheaves are computed affine-locally and localize correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local computation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions involving quasicoherent sheaves that would require sheafification for general sheaves do not require sheafification when considered on the distinguished affine base; injectivity, surjectivity, kernels, tensor products and so on may be computed on affine opens (caveat: Hom has subtleties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever working with quasicoherent sheaves, reduce arguments to affine opens (use the affine communication lemmas/exercises). This simplifies proofs and computations; note the minor caveat concerning Hom (see Exercise 14.3.A referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qcqs Lemma (6.2.8): localization of global sections under quasicompact quasiseparated hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is quasicompact and quasiseparated, and f ∈ Γ(X, OX) is a function. Then the restriction map Γ(X, F) → Γ(X_f, F) is precisely localization, i.e., Γ(X, F)_f ≅ Γ(X_f, F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: translate 'quasicompact quasiseparated' into 'covered by finitely many affines whose pairwise intersections are covered by finitely many affines', apply exactness/localization facts and the exact functor ⊗_{Γ(X,OX)} (Γ(X,OX)_f) to the Cech-style exact sequence arising from a finite affine cover (hint in 6.2.G). The lemma fails without quasicompactness (counterexample: infinite disjoint union of affines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria to check a subcategory is abelian
rubrics_metrics.description: To check that a full subcategory of an ambient abelian category is an abelian subcategory it suffices to check: (i) 0 is in the subcategory; (ii) the subcategory is closed under finite sums; (iii) the subcategory is closed under kernels and cokernels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to QCohX ⊂ ModOX: show 0 is quasicoherent, finite sums of quasicoherent sheaves are quasicoherent (use affines), and that kernels and cokernels of morphisms of quasicoherent sheaves are quasicoherent by checking on affine opens and using localization arguments (Important Exercise 6.2.D). This yields that QCohX is an abelian category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness can be checked affine-locally (6.3.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of quasicoherent sheaves F → G → H on X is exact iff it is exact on every open set in any given affine cover of X. In particular, taking sections over an affine open Spec A is an exact functor from QCoh(X) to A-modules (with the usual left-exact caveat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows checking injectivity/surjectivity of morphisms by passing to an affine cover of your choice. Note the caution: exactness on the right (surjectivity) of the sequence of section functors is only guaranteed when the open is affine; this is the origin of expected higher cohomology (H^1) phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local presentation criterion for quasicoherent sheaves (6.3.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: An OX-module F on a scheme X is quasicoherent iff there exists an open cover by Ui such that on each Ui, F|_{Ui} is isomorphic to the cokernel of a map of two finite-rank free sheaves: O_{Ui}^{⊕I} → O_{Ui}^{⊕J} → F|_{Ui} → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual 'locally cokernel of a map between free sheaves' characterization of quasicoherent sheaves (useful in many contexts, including complex analytic geometry). It provides a concrete local description used in proofs and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness definitions for modules: finitely generated, finitely presented, coherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Three finiteness conditions on an A-module M: (1) finitely generated (there is a surjection A^{⊕p} → M); (2) finitely presented (there exists an exact sequence A^{⊕q} → A^{⊕p} → M → 0 with finite q,p); (3) coherent: M is finitely generated and for every map A^{⊕p} → M the kernel is finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A is Noetherian, these three notions coincide (Proposition 6.4.2). Use these module-theoretic definitions to define finiteness notions for quasicoherent sheaves by checking on affine opens: Γ(Spec A, F) should satisfy the corresponding module condition for every affine Spec A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent modules/sheaves form an abelian subcategory (6.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coherent A-modules form an abelian subcategory of A-modules (and coherent sheaves form an abelian category Coh(X) on a scheme X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify 0 is coherent, closure under finite sums, and closure under kernels/cokernels; over a Noetherian ring kernels of maps between finitely generated modules are finitely generated (Exercise 3.6.Y), which is used to check coherence is preserved under subobjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness properties are affine-local (6.4.A/B/C and 6.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F is finite type (resp. finitely presented, coherent) if for every affine open Spec A, Γ(Spec A, F) is a finitely generated (resp. finitely presented, coherent) A-module. By the Affine Communication Lemma, it suffices to check these properties on the open sets in a single affine cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use localization lemmas (Exercises 6.4.A–6.4.C) and the Affine Communication Lemma 5.3.2 to reduce global finiteness checks to checks on a finite affine cover. Typical proof strategies: localize at elements, use glueing and finiteness-preserving arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: do not equate 'coherent' with 'finitely generated' (6.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not uncommon in the literature to incorrectly define coherent as finitely generated. This is wrong: coherence requires a finiteness condition on kernels of maps from finite free modules as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct definition of coherence to avoid confusion and to identify the minimal hypotheses needed for proofs. This distinction matters outside Noetherian contexts and for non-algebraic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence is not useful in smooth (C^∞) geometry (6.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the local ring O_0 of germs of smooth functions at 0 is not coherent as an O_0-module; there exist non-finitely-generated kernels (explicit construction using a bump-type function φ). Hence the sheaf of smooth functions on R is not coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern for applying algebraic coherence in analytic/smooth settings: do not expect coherence of structure sheaf in smooth manifolds. Use analytic/coherent-analytic notions (Oka's theorem) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan–Hölder theorem and composition series (6.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M (an object of an abelian category) has a finite composition series 0 = M0 ⊂ M1 ⊂ ... ⊂ Mn = M with simple quotients Mi+1/Mi, then any two composition series have the same length and the multiset of simple quotients is the same (up to permutation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: simple object = only subobjects are 0 and itself; finite length = existence of composition series. Consequences include a well-defined length ℓ(M) and multiplicities of simple factors. Proof uses the rectangular array (refinement/intersection) argument and the pattern analysis in 2×2 sub-squares; exercises guide through the complete proof and refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of finite-length modules and their decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite-length A-module M (over a ring A): (a) simple objects in ModA are exactly A/m for maximal ideals m; (b) if M has composition factors A/m_i then M is annihilated by the product m_1...m_n and decomposes via Chinese Remainder into pieces supported at each distinct maximal ideal; (c) M is finitely generated and Supp M is a finite set of closed points; (d) length is additive in short exact sequences and subquotients of finite-length objects have finite length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these properties to analyze support, to define 'length at a point', and to construct idempotent decompositions e_iM of the module. Exercises 6.5.H–6.5.K and 6.5.L–6.5.M develop these facts and their sheaf-theoretic analogues in QCoh(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and key properties of associated primes/points (6.6.5 and 6.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated primes of an A-module M are prime ideals of the form Ann_A(m) for some m∈M; the associated points are the corresponding points of Spec A. For finitely generated M over a Noetherian ring A there are finitely many associated primes, and many additional "zillion properties" hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collected important properties (summarized in the text): Ass_A M is finite for finitely generated M over Noetherian A; Supp M = closure of Ass_A M; the support of any submodule is the closure of a subset of Ass M; Ass behaves well under localization and in exact sequences (Ass of submodule ⊂ Ass of module); an element of A is a zerodivisor iff it vanishes at an associated point; an element is nilpotent iff it vanishes at every associated point; embedded points are associated points contained in closure of others. These properties allow geometric intuition (embedded points, nonreduced loci) and calculations of annihilators and supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support vs annihilator relation (6.6.A and 6.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an element m of an A-module M, Supp(m) = V(Ann_A m). For a finitely generated module M, Supp M is a closed subset of Spec A (and Supp M = Supp M), and support behaves well in exact sequences and under localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relation Supp(m) = V(Ann m) to pass between algebraic annihilators and geometric supports. Exercises illustrate how passing to quotients by elements affects support (e.g., Supp(M/xM) = Supp(M) ∩ V(x) when M is finitely generated). These facts are basic tools for analyzing support and associated primes.
